content.title: About
content.content: Biscuit is a light, airy cake made from eggs, sugar, flour, and a small amount of fat. It has a soft, slightly sweet texture and is often used as a base for cakes, desserts, and layered sweets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Biscuit originated in Europe in the 19th century as a variant of light, leavening‑free cake.
Traditional biscuit is prepared using the “foam” method, where eggs and sugar are beaten into a thick mousse before gently folding in flour.
Biscuit is frequently used in confectionery to create “sponges” – thin layers that can be stacked and shaped into complex structures.
In some countries the biscuit is called a “soft cake” because of its tender crumb.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Classic biscuit contains minimal butter, making it less calorie‑dense than many other cookies.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Biscuit provides a quick source of energy thanks to its simple carbohydrate content.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The porous structure aids digestion, making biscuit suitable for people with sensitive stomachs.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Biscuit is usually made from wheat flour, so it may trigger reactions in individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sugar in biscuit can raise blood glucose levels, so people with diabetes should limit consumption.

items.title: Short shelf life
items.content: Because of its high porosity, biscuit quickly loses moisture and can become dry; store it in an airtight container.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Biscuit can be enjoyed on its own, soaked in syrups, used as a cake base, sliced and served with fruit, berries, cream, or ice cream. It is also commonly layered in desserts such as parfaits.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store biscuit in a sealed container in a cool, dry place. For longer storage keep it in the refrigerator, or freeze it if you need to preserve freshness and prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Cottage cheese is a fresh cheese made from skimmed or partially skimmed milk by curdling and draining the whey. Combined with fruit (such as berries, apples or peaches) it creates a light, nutritious, and tasty snack that is popular in health‑focused diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cottage cheese is one of the oldest dairy products, known to have been made in ancient Egypt.
Unlike most cheeses, cottage cheese is not aged, so it retains most of the milk’s original nutrients.
Fruit‑topped cottage cheese is a common component of traditional dishes worldwide, for example Russian cottage cheese desserts with berries.
Its easy digestibility makes it a frequent choice in children’s meals and post‑illness recovery diets.
Fruit cottage cheese is often served as a dessert, sweetened with honey, nuts or seeds.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Cottage cheese provides high‑quality milk protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Calcium supports bone and tooth health and plays a role in muscle function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Low‑fat cottage cheese contains minimal fat, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Fruit adds fiber and antioxidants
items.content: Fruits such as berries are high in fiber, vitamin C and polyphenols, boosting immunity and protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience bloating, gas, or diarrhea after consuming cottage cheese.

items.title: Milk‑protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein can cause skin rashes, swelling, or even anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some cottage cheese varieties contain added salt, which should be considered by those with hypertension.

items.title: Sugar in fruit
items.content: Sweet fruits raise the glycemic index of the dish, which may be undesirable for diabetics.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cottage cheese with fruit can be enjoyed as a snack, blended into smoothies, used in casseroles, pancakes or as a filling for crepes and waffles. For a smoother taste, it is often mixed with honey or yogurt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cottage cheese in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C. Consume within 3–5 days for best quality. Add fruit just before serving to prevent it from becoming soggy.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken tenders (or strips) are small pieces of chicken breast fillet that are coated in breadcrumbs or batter and fried until golden. The product is often sold frozen and ready to cook in an oven, skillet, or air‑fryer.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tenders are made from the tenderloin of the breast, making them softer than traditional chicken nuggets from thigh meat.
In the United States they are commonly called "chicken strips" or "chicken tenders" and are a staple of fast‑food menus and school cafeterias.
A double coating (flour, egg wash, then breadcrumbs or cornflakes) is used to achieve a crunchy crust.
Frozen tenders usually contain a modest amount of salt and spices, and many brands offer versions without added MSG.
They are often served with barbecue, honey‑mustard, or creamy garlic sauces.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken breast provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with dark‑meat cuts, breast meat contains less saturated fat, especially when cooked with minimal oil.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains niacin (B3), vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Provides phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones, immunity and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: The tender texture and high protein content make it a convenient protein source for children and older adults.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Pre‑seasoned tenders can be high in salt, so intake should be monitored.

items.title: Trans fats in coating
items.content: If the breading is made with partially hydrogenated oils, trans fats may be present.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Like any raw poultry, tenders can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter if not stored or cooked properly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook tenders in a 200 °C oven for 15‑20 minutes, pan‑fry, or air‑fry until crisp. Serve with your favorite dipping sauces, add to salads, wraps, or enjoy as a quick‑meal protein.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen tenders in the freezer at – 18 °C. After thawing, use within 1‑2 days and store in the refrigerator at + 2‑4 °C. Do not leave thawed meat at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

kale-fresh-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Kale, fresh, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala) is a leafy cruciferous vegetable. Fresh kale has dark green, slightly curly leaves with a mildly bitter flavor. When cooked without added fat, it retains most of its nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kale is often called a "superfood" because of its high vitamin and mineral content.
In the wild it grows along the Mediterranean coast and on Atlantic islands.
Leaves can be smooth or curly; curly kale is frequently considered more nutrient‑dense.
Traditional medicine has used kale to support digestion and bone health.
In Japan kale is known as "mizuna" and is a common addition to miso soup.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Kale provides over 700% of the daily value for vitamin K, essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Abundant antioxidants
items.content: Kale contains carotenoids, quercetin, and sulforaphane, which protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain healthy blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Kale supplies calcium, magnesium, and iron, important for bones, muscles, and blood formation.

items.title: Interaction with blood thinners
items.content: The high vitamin K content may reduce the effectiveness of anticoagulant medications.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Kale contains oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: Glucosinolates in kale may affect thyroid function when consumed in very large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Kale can be eaten raw in salads, but for fat‑free cooking steam, blanch, or dry‑sauté it. Remove tough stems, slice the leaves, and season with lemon juice, garlic, or a splash of soy sauce. Cooked kale pairs well with beans, quinoa, or roasted vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh kale in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or wrapped in a damp towel; it stays crisp for 3‑5 days. Cooked kale should be kept in an airtight container in the fridge and consumed within 2‑3 days.
